title: Pericardiocentesis in neonates (tamponade, pneumopericardium)
subject: paediatrics
summary: Suspect tamponade in any neonate with a UVC or PICC who suddenly deteriorates. Confirm with bedside echo, remove or reposition the line, and if the heart is compressed drain by ultrasound-guided subxiphoid puncture with a 22G cannula aimed at the left shoulder, aspirating as you advance.

sections.title: Suspect it
items: Central catheters (UVC or PICC) can perforate the thin preterm myocardium or vessel wall; a tip in or against the right atrium is the main risk. Mechanical tip damage and hypertonic fluid are both implicated.
Signs are non-specific: sudden rise in oxygen need, tachycardia, poor perfusion, an enlarged cardiac silhouette, or cardiac arrest.
PICC tips move: up to 24% migrate within 24 hours, and perforation has occurred with tips outside the cardiac silhouette.
Symptomatic pneumopericardium in a ventilated baby can quickly become life-threatening and needs urgent drainage.

sections.title: Confirm
items: Use bedside echo (POCUS): it shows the effusion, chamber compression and the catheter tip (subxiphoid and parasternal views).
Chest X-ray is poor at separating effusion from the heart shadow; ultrasound is preferred.

sections.title: Drain
items: When echo shows chamber compression, restricted filling and low cardiac output, do pericardiocentesis promptly. The subxiphoid percutaneous approach is safer and more reliable.

Technique: insert a 22G peripheral cannula below the xiphoid, aim toward the left shoulder and aspirate as you advance, under ultrasound guidance. One preterm case used a 21-gauge needle on a 10 mL syringe and improved after 4 mL of air was aspirated.

Deal with the line: a malpositioned UVC was removed immediately in a POCUS case series; small effusions resolved after repositioning the tip. Draining the effusion through the PICC and pulling the tip back from the atrium have also been reported.
If the pericardium holds clot or the baby stays unstable, surgical subxiphoid pericardial drainage may be needed.

sections.title: After drainage
items: Send the fluid for biochemistry: effusions from central lines are often parenteral nutrition (35 mL of TPN-like fluid in one UVC case; 17 mL of chylous fluid in one PICC case).
Repeat echo to watch for re-accumulation, and keep continuous ECG monitoring.

sections.title: Prevention
items: Keep PICC tips in the vena cava outside the heart: about 1 cm beyond the cardiac silhouette in preterm and 2 cm in term infants. Check the tip by X-ray or ultrasound at least twice a week.
Aim UVC tips at the junction of the IVC and right atrium, and use POCUS to watch for migration.
